[Paper Summary]

 The paper presents the Catechol Benchmark, a novel transient-flow dataset for solvent selection and yield prediction in chemistry. It provides >1200 continuous-condition measurements and benchmarks multiple ML methods.

[Assessment of Reviews]

 Reviewers were overall positive (scores: 5, 4, 5, 4). Strengths include the novelty and quality of the dataset, and clear relevance to ML for chemistry. Concerns raised were dataset size, limited reaction scope, and modest exploration of advanced baselines. The rebuttal addressed these points well, and reviewers generally maintained or improved their scores.

[Justification for Decision]

Given the novelty, open availability, and positive reception, I recommend acceptance. While some limitations remain (dataset size, scope, and baselines), they are outweighed by the potential impact of this dataset.

[Comment]

 For the camera-ready, the authors should expand code documentation, include solvent sustainability details, and clarify dataset curation and outlier handling.

Thank you kindly for your careful review, and for recognizing the relevance and value of this work.

> more advanced and recently proposed methods [in active learning]

Due to the expensive experimentation, process condition datasets such as ours tend to lie in the low-data regime. This makes low-data models such as Gaussian processes the most suitable model type, and therefore we focus on the standard active learning methods in low-data settings.

Other methods such as Corset and BADGE, focus on much larger batch data labeling for deep learning models. A lot of the times the methods are focused on Convolutional Neural Networks for image classification, which does not apply in our case. Furthermore, the total number of data-points acquired in the active learning procedure lie in the tens of thousands, as opposed to less than 100 in our case.

We believe we benchmarked the appropriate methods for our case, but we do recognize that research in settings such as ours is focused far more on Bayesian optimization than active learning. With this mind, we further add a more practical example, where we consider a multi-objective optimization problem, where we try to find the Pareto front between yield, selectivity, and solvent greenness. We showcase results for different multi-objective optimization metrics in Tables 2, 3, and 4.

> regression benchmarking is overly centered on Gaussian Processes.

We agree with the reviewer, unfortunately we were resource-constrained and could not carry out the fine-tuning of the LLM models. However, we do believe the dataset is small enough that small data approaches such as GPs are more suitable, which is why they were our main focus. Moreover, the fact that GPs require little tuning is a strength, as tuning the deep learning methods with e.g. cross-validation would require partitioning the dataset such that even less training data can be used.

Nonetheless, the strong performance of a simple MLP showcases the promise of deep learning in the area, and we hope further research will allow for more general chemistry models to provide strong performance without the need of extensive fine-tuning.

> The dataset focuses on only two reaction types, limiting the scope of generalization.

We feel that this is a necessary trade-off when producing a high-quality dataset, sacrificing breadth for specificity.

The flow set-up we use to generate the data has the benefit of allowing for fine-grained and dense investigation of continuous variables, but struggles with discrete variables, where high-throughput experimentation (HTE) is much stronger.

We therefore focus on settings that work to the strength of this set-up, resulting in an in-depth investigation of only two reaction types. A recent position paper by ORD in fact requested this type of data due to how rare it is to find open-source datasets [1]. We see our paper as an important first-step in addressing this call.

Thank you for your review, and for the constructive feedback on our work.

> repeated measurements 

The repeated measurements are a by-product of having to wait for the reactor to be at steady-state and for all the relevant data to be collected before the next transient flow ramp. We agree that it can lead to certain redundancies, however, we would argue it also allows us to get estimates of the noise levels observed at each solvent, allowing for the hetero-skedastic nature of the problem to be better explored.

 >  Sustainable solvents and complex mixtures are notably underrepresented, limiting broader applicability.

On the contrary, we believe the number of green solvents is over-represented, as we made particularly sure to investigate them. Based on the GSK solvent selection guide [2]: 7 out of 23 solvents are considered green; another 7 can be considered green in the right circumstances (as long as other issues are mitigated, e.g. flammability); 5 are not present on the guide so would require further investigation; and only 4 are considered fully non-green solvents.

Further, regarding complex mixtures, we note that mixtures of two solvents is already a sufficiently complex task. Single solvents, and two-solvent mixtures, cover a significant breadth of chemistry.

However, the reviewer makes a good point that we provide no information about which solvents are green, and to what extent. We will now include Table 1 in the paper and dataset to include information on the solvents. We further highlight the application area by benchmarking a multi-objective Bayesian optimisation (MOBO) algorithm, which seeks to find the Pareto front between total yield, selectivity and solvent greenness. We showcase the different MOBO performance metrics in Tables 2, 3, and 4.

> Key details about how the dataset was curated... are missing

We strongly agree with the reviewer that these key details should be in the paper, and will be included in the camera ready version. The most vital pipeline parameters relate to laboratory set-up, and are provided in the Appendix in section B.1, including all the reactor lengths, the equipment used, and the methods required to replicate the data. This fulfills the recently published ORD schema on transient flow datasets [1]. We believe the results should be easily reproducible by any flow chemist.

Regarding outlier removal, the only points that we collected that were removed from the dataset were those that experience a step-up in flow-rate when they were in the reactor, as per [3]. We will make this clear, and provide more pipeline hyper-parameter details.

When evaluating the ML models, we omitted the acetic acid points for reasons discussed in the paper. Otherwise, we used the full dataset. We include points that could be considered outliers to assess how the ML methods handle such points.

> Catechol and Phenyl Ether subsets differ in conditions and protocols.

While the set-ups were not exact, we believe the transfer learning approach to be valid, and do not expect the conditions and protocols to make much difference. The data is collected in similar flow reactors, which allow for very close control of temperature and other reactions conditions. This means that we operate in a scheme where heat and mass transfer conditions can be considered negligible, and therefore we operate in perfect conditions for the transfer learning to relate to true chemical patterns.

Thank you for your thorough review of our work.

> ...low amount of data...

We accept that many modern approaches perform well when given more data. However, we think this low-data setting is a strength for our dataset: when new chemistry is carried out in a wet lab, very few observations are taken, so our benchmark encourages the development of methods that can empower chemists to explore new reactions.

Additionally, the data on continuous reaction conditions is so rarely available because it is so difficult to obtain. The generation of large datasets on time-series process conditions will require many years of collective effort. A recent position paper by ORD in fact requested this type of data due to how rare it is to find open-source datasets [1]. We see our paper as an important first-step in addressing this call. 

We encourage machine learning practitioners to augment their models with additional data available elsewhere (such as by learning better solvent representations), enabling data-hungry models to still perform well when predicting on our dataset.

> ...usefulness of performing [LLM] experiment without any fine tuning.

We agree with the reviewer, unfortunately we were resource-constrained and could not carry out the fine-tuning of the LLM models. However, we do believe the dataset is small enough that small data approaches such as GPs are more suitable, which is why they were our main focus.

> ...the exact laboratory setup used for data creation is protected by proprietary IP and is not provided...

The laboratory set-up was provided in the Appendix in section B.1, including all the reactor lengths, the equipment used, and the methods required to replicate the data. This fulfills the recently published ORD schema on transient flow datasets [1]. We believe the results should be easily reproducible by any flow chemist.

> code doesn't seem to be well documented

Our repository has a README file describing installation instructions, and the dataset. The scripts also have a minimal amount of self-documentation, due to the use of argparse. For example, one can run `python scripts\eval_single_solvents.py -h` to see the options and a brief description.

However, we agree that further documentation will aid other researchers in building from our code.
Upon publishing our dataset, we will create another README in the eval scripts folder to explain how to use the scripts, as well as further expanding the help text described above.

[1] Deadman, Benjamin J. "WANTED: Flow Chemistry Reaction Data." Chimia 79.6 (2025): 390-395.

We kindly thank the reviewer for their evaluation of our work.

> Limited Reaction Scope

We feel that this is a necessary trade-off when producing a high-quality dataset, sacrificing breadth for specificity.

Also, we argue that most chemistry isn't generalizable. Instead, we want to give a real test case with which we can evaluate ML methods, which could give an indication whether those methods are generalizable.

> Dataset Size

We accept that many modern approaches perform well when given more data. However, we think this low-data setting is a strength for our dataset: when new chemistry is carried out in a wet lab, very few observations are taken, so our benchmark encourages the development of methods that can empower chemists to explore new reactions.

Additionally, the data on continuous reaction conditions is so rarely available because it is so difficult to obtain. The generation of large datasets on time-series process conditions will require many years of collective effort. A recent position paper by ORD in fact requested this type of data due to how rare it is to find open-source datasets [1]. We see our paper as an important first-step in addressing this call. 

We encourage machine learning practitioners to augment their models with additional data available elsewhere (such as by learning better solvent representations), enabling data-hungry models to still perform well when predicting on our dataset.

> Omitted Side‑Reactions

We only remove one solvent during our evaluations. The methods we used in this work are unable to predict these side reactions, and so the computational results were difficult to interpret with this included.

We do also include this solvent in the published dataset, such that any future work can evaluate robustness by including these data.

In practice, the reactions in almost every solvent will contain side-reactions, however, it is very difficult and expensive to know what these are. It would require first identifying the product of the side-reaction, then isolating it in a large enough quantity to then be used for a calibration. This would be extremely expensive and require many many manual hours. Any large dataset of process conditions will ignore side-reactions for this reason, and like us, focuses on the amount of target product generated instead.

Our regression analysis does indeed focus on yield of each of the products, to simplify comparisons between the different method. The other metrics mentioned by the reviewer can be obtained from the dataset, and we encourage practitioners to make full use of the data for downstream applications.

summary.value: The "Catechol Benchmark" introduces a novel, open dataset for yield prediction in laboratory chemistry, specifically focusing on solvent selection. It is the first-ever transient flow dataset for machine learning benchmarking, encompassing over 1200 process conditions. Unlike prior chemical datasets that often deal with discrete parameters, this dataset uniquely provides dense measurements across continuous reaction conditions, such as residence time, temperature, and solvent composition. The authors benchmark several ML algorithms using this dataset.

strengths_contributions.value:
It is a novel and unique dataset that presents new challenges for ML models compared to previous datasets focusing on discrete parameters, such as non-stationarity and heteroskedasticity.

The dataset is appropriately used to benchmark algorithms for design of experiments, demonstrating that active learning criteria (entropy and mutual information) can reduce MSE, and that Bayesian optimization algorithms can quickly identify optimal configurations.

The paper shows a strong engagement with literature at the intersection of chemistry and ML; e.g., extensively discusses "solvent featurization methods" with techniques like reaction fingerprinting and molecular fingerprints.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
Despite its size relative to previous datasets, the 1227 data points are considered a relatively low amount of data for many modern ML approaches.

Directly using LLM embeddings led to poor performance in regression tasks, though fine-tuning is proposed as a potential solution for future work. The paper notes that this poor performance of unfine-tuned LLMs has been reported previously, so it is not clear to me what was the usefulness of performing this experiment without any fine tuning.

Although the data is open, the exact laboratory setup used for data creation is protected by proprietary IP and is not provided, which will complicate attempts to replicate the experimental conditions used for data generation.

dataset_code_comments.value: Data and code available; code doesn't seem to be well documented (e.g., not readme files or documentation for eval scripts).

summary.value: This paper introduces the Catechol Benchmark, a transient‐flow dataset of 1,227 time‐series measurements for allyl‐substituted catechol yield prediction across varied solvent mixtures, temperatures, and residence times, plus a smaller phenyl ether subset. It benchmarks Gaussian Processes, MLPs, Neural ODE variants, and fine-tuned reaction-fingerprint embeddings, proposes GP kernel extensions and transfer learning, and demonstrates active-learning and Bayesian optimization for experimental design.

strengths_contributions.value:
1.  The paper is the first publicly released dense transient‐flow dataset enabling ML on truly continuous reaction spaces.

2. Systematic comparison of classical (GP), neural (MLP, NODE/EODE/LODE), and pretrained-embedding (ChemBERTa, RXNFP) approaches is evaluated with the proposed benchmark.

3.  The paper presents clear demonstrations that information-driven sampling (entropy, MI, EI, UCB) outperforms random selection in both yield modeling and reaction optimization.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1.  While the dataset includes repeated measurements (e.g., 656 single-solvent points under identical conditions), it remains unclear whether these repetitions provide meaningful variability or introduce redundancy, especially given the limited reaction types.

2.  The dataset includes a few examples relevant to solvent replacement or green chemistry. Sustainable solvents and complex mixtures are notably underrepresented, limiting broader applicability.

3.  Key details about how the dataset was curated, such as criteria for excluding invalid points or handling outliers, are missing, along with the pipeline hyperparameters.

4.  The Catechol and Phenyl Ether subsets differ in conditions and protocols. Without proper alignment, jointly training on both may lead models to learn dataset-specific artifacts rather than true chemical patterns.

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

final_justification.value: Most of my original concerns have been sufficiently addressed in the rebuttal, particularly regarding dataset curation transparency, solvent coverage, and reproducibility. The authors clarified key methodological points and added relevant benchmarking. I’m increasing my score to 4.

summary.value: This work presents **The Catechol Benchmark**, the first publicly available, machine‑learning‑ready transient flow dataset for solvent‑selection yield prediction in flow chemistry. It comprises 1,227 densely sampled data points over continuous process conditions (temperature, residence time) and solvent mixtures for the uni‑molecular allyl‑substituted catechol reaction, plus an auxiliary dataset of 283 points on a related ether reaction. The authors benchmark a wide range of regression models (Gaussian processes, neural nets, latent ODEs, LLM embeddings) and solvent featurizations, demonstrate active‑learning and Bayesian‑optimization use cases, and release all data, code, and experimental details for reproducibility.

strengths_contributions.value:
**1. Novel, High‑Quality Dataset**: The dataset is the first to provide continuous kinetic data (temperature, residence time) and solvent‑ramping measurements, addressing a key gap in existing reaction benchmarks that use only discrete conditions.

**2. Comprehensive Benchmarking**: The work systematically evaluates state‑of‑the‑art regression techniques—including GPs with advanced kernels, neural ODEs, and fine‑tuned LLM embeddings—highlighting both successes and failure modes in this dynamic setting.

**3. Machine‑Learning Challenges Identified**: The paper surfaces core difficulties—non‑stationarity, heteroskedasticity, and solvent‑featurization bias—that hinder current models, guiding future method development.

**4. Reproducibility  and Open Science**: All datasets are available on Kaggle with clear documentation, and the accompanying codebase (including active‑learning and BO scripts) is fully open‑source, with detailed appendices and containerized environments for replication.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
**1. Limited Reaction Scope**: The benchmark covers only two reaction systems (catechol and ether), which may constrain generalization to other chemistries or reaction classes.

**2. Dataset Size**: With 1,227 points, the dataset sits at the lower bound for modern ML methods; while adequate for low‑data models like GPs, it may be insufficient to fully assess deep learning approaches without further data augmentation.

**3. Omitted Side‑Reactions**:  Data points involving unintended side reactions (e.g., acetic‑acid cases) were removed, leaving a cleaner but potentially less realistic dataset that does not capture critical failure modes.

**4. Focus on Yield Prediction Only**: The benchmark emphasizes yield as the sole output metric; other critical reaction aspects (selectivity, rate constants, impurity profiles) are not addressed, limiting the breadth of downstream applications.

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

final_justification.value: This work presents a high-quality, first-of-its-kind benchmark dataset for solvent-selection yield prediction under continuous flow conditions, addressing a significant gap in chemical machine learning. With thorough model evaluations, insightful analysis of learning challenges, and strong commitment to open science, I believe the paper meets the standard for acceptance.

summary.value: This paper presents a novel and well-documented dataset—Catechol Benchmark—for benchmarking machine learning models in chemical reaction yield prediction under transient flow conditions. The dataset is focused on the challenging task of solvent selection, offering dense, time-series measurements across continuous parameters such as temperature, residence time, and solvent ratios. The authors benchmark several regression models and solvent featurizations, and explore active learning and Bayesian optimization scenarios using the data.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. The paper is clearly written and well-organized.

2. The research problem is highly relevant to the chemical sciences, especially in the context of sustainable solvent replacement, which is a pressing need in modern chemical manufacturing.

3. The released dataset is valuable, providing dense and high-quality experimental data that fills a gap in ML-ready chemistry benchmarks.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. Active learning is a key component of this work, but the selection criteria explored are limited to entropy-based acquisition. The paper would benefit from comparisons with more advanced and recently proposed methods such as Coreset, BADGE, and gradient-based or submodular acquisition strategies. Notably, several competitive methods were proposed recently (e.g., [https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.00334]) and should be considered for a more convincing benchmark.

2. The regression benchmarking is overly centered on Gaussian Processes. While GP-based modeling is appropriate in low-data scenarios, the deep learning baselines (e.g., MLP, ChemBERTa-https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.09885) are not sufficiently explored or optimized, and the paper lacks ablation or tuning analysis to show their true potential.

3. The dataset focuses on only two reaction types, limiting the scope of generalization. Expanding to a wider set of reaction mechanisms would improve the robustness and broader applicability of the benchmark.

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

additional_feedback.value: While the benchmark is indeed valuable, this paper can be further improved with more advanced AI baselines.

final_justification.value: The author's responses have addressed my concerns and made me more confident in my evaluation. I choose to maintain my positive scores.

title.value: The Catechol Benchmark: Time-series Solvent Selection Data for Few-shot Machine Learning

TLDR.value: We introduce the first ever transient flow dataset for benchmarking ML for chemistry, focusing on time-series data for solvent selection.

abstract.value: Machine learning has promised to change the landscape of laboratory chemistry, with impressive results in molecular property prediction and reaction retro-synthesis. However, chemical datasets are often inaccessible to the machine learning community as they tend to require cleaning, thorough understanding of the chemistry, or are simply not available. In this paper, we introduce a novel dataset for yield prediction, providing the first-ever transient flow dataset for machine learning benchmarking, covering over 1200 process conditions. While previous datasets focus on discrete parameters, our experimental set-up allow us to sample a large number of continuous process conditions, generating new challenges for machine learning models. We focus on solvent selection, a task that is particularly difficult to model theoretically and therefore ripe for machine learning applications. We showcase benchmarking for regression algorithms, transfer-learning approaches, feature engineering, and active learning, with important applications towards solvent replacement and sustainable manufacturing.
